en: The Itihāsopaniṣad. Om. The lineage of Śibi was indeed the lineage of Vṛṣādarvi. This history (itihāsa) became the family lore (kulavidyā) of that [lineage]. Whosoever used to study this, he would become a king. Having attained something, he disappeared. He said: "To whoever shall teach me this history, I will grant a boon. Then a Brahmin entered into a union with him. A person, sun-colored like the sun, emerged from the sun and caused him to learn it. He asked him: *Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.*

"Who are you? or "Vṛṣādarvi. Therefore, he who studies this ancient narrative (itihāsa) becomes one who moves at will in the world of Āditya. Therefore, a young Brāhmaṇa who has been initiated should learn this ancient narrative; having learned it, he should then recite it to the Brāhmaṇas. He shall become wise, live for a hundred years, and master the Veda with its six auxiliary limbs. Therefore, he who recites this ancient narrative should offer a handful of water to the ancestors.

Rivers with banks of cakes and mud of ghee and milk-rice should appear before him. Therefore, whoever should offer a *śrāddha* to the ancestors while reciting this history (*itihāsa*), it will be as if a *gayā-śrāddha* has been performed on a grand scale. "Svadhā" belongs to the ancestors; thus, for his ancestors, there is infinite satisfaction. Whoever knows this—this very history is auspicious, meritorious, conducive to obtaining sons, conducive to cattle, conducive to long life, and conducive to heaven; it grants liberation from all fears at all times.

There is no fear from natural calamities; none from thieves; none from demons. One does not perish on a journey; one does not perish in water; one does not perish in fire. One is not slain by water nor by a weapon. One does not die childless. By reciting it in the evening, one destroys the evil committed during the day; by reciting it in the morning, one destroys the evil committed during the night. By reciting it both in the evening and in the morning, even a sinner becomes sinless.

For indeed, the sinners depart from those listeners who are free from malice, while they share in the merit [of the teaching]. There are one hundred and one other virtuous traditional scriptures; such is the extent of this exposition. Beyond this, one should know:
"The tongue perceives taste, the heart experiences what is dear, the eye is the portion that witnesses what is seen, and through the mind one sees clearly."
By the mind one guides speech; by the eye the world is measured;
the two ears are the hearers of what has come to be; food is commensurate with the vital breath.
Food is life; Parjanya, the son of Vṛṣādarvi, has bestowed this great gift.
Agni, the bearer of oblations, has accepted it; this very thing, O cows, is the sacrificial offering.
Wealth, kin, the lineage of progeny, the form of ritual action, and the great friend—
wisdom is the foundation of these threads, while sacrifices and charitable works are their ultimate refuge.
They speak the truth; they carry across falsehood; they drink milk; they drink honey;
they drink Soma together with immortality; beyond death, they become immortal.
Those Brahmins who practice the holy life (brahmacarya)—for indeed, they say, this history (itihāsa) is equal in measure to the Veda.
He practices dharma and not adharma; he speaks truth and not falsehood.
He looks to the long-term and not the short-term; he looks to what is supreme and not the inferior.
He who knows the Ṛg-verses knows the gods; he who knows the Yajus-formulas knows the sacrifice;
he who knows the Sāman-chants knows all; and he who knows the mental [sacrifice] knows Brahman.
He who remains angry when another is angry incurs excessive speech;
he who leads one to excessive speech indeed knows all that is mental, for so we have heard from the twice-born.
Austerity is the limit, faith is the supreme mother, and truth they call his father;
yoga is his self, conduct is his kinsman, and self-restraint is the foundation—not the earth—for the wise man.
Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, and death again and again is suffering;
the cycle of existence is suffering, wherein living beings are cooked.
That Brahmin who, though a doer of evil, is a composer of mantras, lives on;
devoted to the Veda and a performer of sacred rites, he is eternally honored in the world of Brahmā.
Grasses desire only to be *kuśa* grass; trees desire to be sacrificial posts; and cattle desire to be cows.
O King, all living beings desire the status of a Brahmin; there is nothing superior to being a Brahmin.
A hundred Āhāvas, a hundred Śaras, a hundred Ṛjīṣins,
a hundred Brahmins, and a hundred ascetics abide in a well of the forest.
The cave is covered by truth; the cave is covered by what has been heard;
the cave is covered by mindfulness; the cave is covered by tranquility.
The cave is covered by Dama; the cave is covered by Satya.
The cave is covered by the Self; the cave is covered by Brahman.
O Brahmin, those who perceive the treasure within their minds, seeing both the hidden lower and the higher,
who are travelers on the paths without being mere wayfarers and who reach the further shore— they are the true Brāhmaṇas, equal to the sun.
He who performs śrāddha rites without attachment does not travel by the path of the gods;
like a pipal fruit released from its bond, he falls away from the heavenly world, being a friend to those who perform no śrāddha.
May we partake of that oblation which is the fulfiller of the sacrifice, the thread offered among the gods;
for one who does not know the Veda does not comprehend this Great One.
The self is the enjoyer of all in the world beyond;
this is the eternal greatness of the Brahmin:
he does not increase by action, nor does he become diminished.
Having known the path and the state of that very Self,
one is not smeared by evil action.
The Agnihotra fire, aged oxen, a guest who has arrived at the proper time,
children, and the elders of the family— these burn [the house] when they are treated with contempt.
The alms called *saṃbhojanī* are the food of Piśācas; they go neither to the ancestors nor to the gods.
Having its merit exhausted, it wanders right here like a cow that has lost its calf wandering within a stall.
That twice-born man who, having eaten at a śrāddha, emits semen upon a Śūdra woman,
sprinkles his ancestors with semen severed from the womb of a Śūdra.
If a twice-born man, deluded by lust, procreates a son upon a Śūdra woman,
he shall remain in that most dreadful state for as long as it takes for that son to be born upon the earth.
When one feeds a Brāhmaṇa who is unlearned in the Vedas, the ancestors do not eat at sixteen successive Śrāddha rites;
consequently, the ancestors become hopeless, and the gods, together with Indra, hurl their thunderbolt.
Indeed, as many morsels of sacrificial oblation as that man-eater consumes,
so many spikes does he swallow upon reaching Yama, the son of Vivasvat;
they cut the hand of the donor and the tip of the tongue of the other.
If one offers a funeral feast (śrāddha) purified by mantras to one who does not know the mantras,
or if an ascetic (yati) appointed to the rite should discard meat during the offering to the gods,
he shall fall into hell for as many years as there are hairs on the body of that animal.
O Lord of Men, just as seed sown in barren soil does not yield a share of the harvest for the sower,
so too a funeral rite (*śrāddha*) that lacks a firm foundation perishes.
Having performed and partaken of a *śrāddha*, one should not engage in social intercourse.
For that month, his ancestors subsist on semen.
Having given and having eaten at a śrāddha,
the ancestors eat the remnants of the performer for six months, along with those who sat in the same row and those who ate together.
If one who has eaten at a *śrāddha* feast, being deluded by greed, should eat again at another *śrāddha*,
that *śrāddha* becomes nullified and he shall go to the Raurava hell.
Having both given and eaten at a *śrāddha*, the twice-born man merely bears a heavy burden.
For one month, his ancestors remain oppressed by the burden [of that food].
But for him who, having offered the *śrāddha* and having eaten, sets out on a journey,
his ancestors remain for that month subsisting on dust.
One who lacks the Veda has no sacred fire; one devoid of the Veda is likewise without fire.
Even one who possesses the sacred fire is without it if he has not studied the Veda; such a person is traditionally considered to be without fire.
One should not cause the remains of food to be given to women, Śūdras, children, and the like.
Even if one should give it through negligence, it does not reach those ancestors.
One who maintains the sacred fires is always a worthy recipient, and one who knows the Vedas is always a worthy recipient;
yet the most excellent of all recipients is he in whose stomach the food of a Śūdra has never entered.

Furthermore, one who has eaten at a funeral feast (śrāddha) should avoid these eight things: eating again, traveling on a journey, carrying a load, Vedic study, sexual union, giving gifts, receiving gifts, and performing fire-offerings (homa).
One who performs the cleaning of teeth, the chewing of betel, or the cutting of nails and hair on the previous day shall indeed become an eater [of the funeral feast] on the following day.
The performer of a Śrāddha should avoid brushing the teeth, betel nut, shaving, oil massage, eating, sexual intercourse, medicinal drugs, and food provided by others.
If a performer of a śrāddha ceremony greedily eats at another's śrāddha,
that śrāddha becomes ruined and he shall go to the Raurava hell.
If one eats again after having been invited and the guest has already departed,
he performs the same karma as a vulture does through its association with village swine.
In accepting gifts, one suffers poverty, and his giving becomes fruitless; by performing fire-sacrifices, he may become afflicted with leprosy, and through Vedic recitations, he may meet death.
Know that for a man who eats without reciting the Ṛg-verses, his only wealth is the Brahman alone.
Dharma moves within the ancestral offering (svadhā) and bestows it; truth is the sweetest of all flavors.
Truth is the preeminence among the sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis), and likewise, wisdom is the seventh among the means of life.
There is no transgression against a Brahmin; a fool should avoid [reciting] a mantra. For one does not offer oblations into ashes after having cast away a blazing fire.

A Brāhmaṇa who knows the mantras and is purified by a single [gift] is worthy of all that one might offer at a Śrāddha ceremony even if he were to perform it for a hundred thousand times ten thousand.
Having eaten at seven or nine thousand Brāhmaṇas, one becomes a knower and a meditator; of this there is no doubt. Whose food remains in the stomach, that is digested through the study of the Vedas.
It delivers their family—ten ancestors and ten descendants.

The Brāhmaṇa is the best among bipeds; the cow is the best among quadrupeds; gold is the best among metals. As oil is in sesame seeds and clarified butter in curds, as fire is in the friction-sticks and in flowing water, so does the Self arise within the self. One perceives it rightly through a truthful mind; by means of a truthful mind, one directs speech toward it.
The gods, facing eastward, receive the oblation, and the ancestors, facing northward.
They accept [the gift] from a crowded place, from fire, and from a Brāhmaṇa.
That Brahmin who constantly studies the Vedas, remains steadfast as a Brāhmaṇa, observes proper conduct, and maintains the sacred fire—he is indeed Agni Kavyavāhana.
One should offer the *vikira* by scattering it; for one should eat the *vikira* while scattering it, demonstrating the various forms of satisfaction.
One should indeed give [the offerings] in an enclosed space, for the ancestors are traditionally considered to be modest;
all ancestors are eaters of raw flesh, yet they are fond of sesame, light, and ghee.
The place, the time, the recipient, the mantra, the eightfold purity, the desire for merit, the waning of the dark fortnight, and festivals;

the remains of food, the offerings made to Śiva, vomit, and the shroud of the deceased—these seven are pure at a *śrāddha*. Furthermore, the daughter's son, the *kutapa* woolen cloth, and sesame seeds [are also pure].
Three things are purifying at a Śrāddha: a daughter’s son, a Kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds.
And three things they praise here: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of envy.
When the sun grows dim during the eighth part of the day—
That time is called *kutapa*; what is given to the ancestors during it becomes inexhaustible.
A wise man, having commenced the *śrāddha* at *kutapa*, should perform its conclusion (*ārohaṇa*) by following the prescribed rule; one who knows the ritual must not overstep the *rauhiṇī* hour.
If one should cross the Rauhiṇī, whether intentionally or even unintentionally, that śrāddha becomes demonic; it does not reach the ancestors.
Yātudhānas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and likewise Asuras—
these indeed carry off the Śrāddha where one performs the rite for the gods.
If one were to omit the portion for the gods in a śrāddha, it becomes a rākṣasa rite;
there, rākṣasas and piśācas [prevail], and no person feels aversion toward it.
The gods enter from the front; one should dismiss the god from behind.
A cock destroys [the merit] by its wings, while a pig does so by its snout. A dog destroys it by its arrival, and the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) by his very glance.
One should avoid giving a daughter in marriage to, performing ancestral śrāddha rites for, or even offering salutations to one whose country, name, and lineage (for three generations) are unknown.
He whose Veda and sacrificial altar are lost for three generations is indeed called a "wicked Brāhmaṇa," excluded from all ritual acts.
An eight-year-old girl is a *kanyā*, a nine-year-old is a *rohiṇī*, and a ten-year-old is a *gaurī*; beyond this age, she is *rajasvalā* (menstruating).
A maiden who sees her menses while still in her father’s house and remains unconsecrated by marriage is called a *vṛṣalī*; her husband is a *vṛṣalīpati*.
The ancestors do not accept śrāddha offerings or sacrificial oblations consumed by the husband of a vṛṣalī woman, and the giver does not go to heaven.
A wife is called *mahiṣī*; wealth acquired through her is *bhaga*.
He who subsists upon that property is indeed known as a *māhiṣika*.
He who, having taken up wealth at a low price, gives it back at a high price,
is indeed called a usurer and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
Having seen first a keeper of prostitutes, then a husband of a low-caste woman in the middle,
and finally a usurer at the end, the ancestors departed in despair.

One who has white leprosy, one with skin disease, likewise one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is one-eyed, one who is lame, and one who is the son of a remarried woman;

One who has broken his vow of chastity, one born from a *kuṇḍa* or *golaka* womb, a professional soldier, an adulterer, one who teaches for a fee, a eunuch, a defiler of virgins, and one who is falsely accused.
One who betrays friends, a slanderer, a seller of the Vedas, one who reviles the Vedas,
one who abandons mother, father, or guru, one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*, and the son of a *vṛṣala* woman.

One who has previously been married to another, one born of a Śūdra woman, one who has sexual intercourse with a menstruating woman, and those who cause harm to others— these are excluded from the śrāddha rite.
The slayer of gods or Brahmins, and those who steal their property—these qualities must not be mentioned; they are excluded from the śrāddha rite.
One should feed one's brothers at the śrāddha, or even a son endowed with good qualities;
or one may eat oneself, but never a Brahmin devoid of Vedic knowledge.
If a śrāddha is offered to them, that śrāddha becomes fruitless;
the ancestors depart from him disappointed, along with the gods and the ṛṣis.
That twice-born man who, through delusion or lust, procreates a son upon a Śūdra woman,
shall remain in this most dreadful state for as long as he remains upon the earth.
Whether it be milk, curd, oil, buttermilk, clarified butter, or honey—
a Brahmin who sells these shall go to the Raurava hell.
One should eat with speech restrained as long as the food is still warm;
the ancestors consume it only so long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been described.
The qualities of the sacrificial offering should not be mentioned as long as the ancestors have not yet been presented with it;
once the ancestors are satisfied, one may afterwards say that the offering was excellent.
He who knows this goddess here— who is established in all beings as the existent one—
neither sorrows nor griefs behold his heart.
Neither wife nor children, nor cattle, can rescue one from what has been committed.
The essence of water, honey, clarified butter, milk, and of food that has been prepared—
these essences reach the Śrāddha of those who are restrained in speech and gathered together, through the essence of all essences.

"Rise, O Sun! Choose a boon," the king said. "These five jewels [I possess]: my cow yields milk for me perpetually; my oblation-gathering [cow] gathers the sacrificial food for me perpetually; my splendor grinds for me perpetually; my chariot traverses all the oceans; and these two jeweled earrings are the color of the sun. "Then choose one of these indeed," [the Sun said]. The Brahmin said, "Wait until I have consulted [my family]. He consulted his wife. His wife said, "Take the sacrificial food. He consulted his son.

"Take the chariot," said the son. He asked the daughter; "The jeweled earrings," said the daughter. He asked the slave-girl; "Take the grindstone," said the slave-girl. Without approaching, Havirbhārī said: "The son desires the chariot, the daughter the jeweled earrings, the slave-girl the grindstone, and I, O Śibi, the seventh, desire the cow. "I give you all these indeed," said Vṛṣādarvi. This very thing is the ancient legend (itihāsa) that Brahmā told to Āditya, and Āditya to Puroga, and Puroga to Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa [gave it] to Bharadvāja; Bharadvāja [gave it] to many [disciples], including several great kings. From there, the twice-born Dhanapati, born in a Brāhmaṇa family, became [the recipient].
One who is liberated from the sins committed over seven lifetimes by means of the sacred festival days (parvan) remains with the ancestors in their abode whenever the sun is situated in Virgo.
Day by day, [the merit] is equal to that of Gayā at Bharaṇī and at Gayapañcaka;
it is tenfold at Vyatīpāta, and twentyfold during the middle of the fortnight.
They say that on the twelfth day one obtains a hundredfold merit, and on the new moon day, a thousandfold;
but on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, the fruit is ten thousandfold.
Whether with cooked food, or with vegetables, roots, or fruits— therefore, with every effort, one should perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha.
The city of the hungry ghosts (pretas) there remains empty until the sight of a scorpion;
when the scorpions come into view, the ancestors depart, having lost all hope.
Then, having pronounced a most dreadful curse, some ancestors say as they depart for their own abode, "Alas! This should not have been spoken."
Those who are childless and without cattle exist in this world as objects of reproach;
they dwell in the terrible Raurava hell until the dissolution of all beings.
One should desire many sons, so that even one of them might go to Gayā,
or perform a horse sacrifice, or release a bull as a mark of devotion.
A bull that is white from its two horns, with a pale-white face and tail,
and red in color, is called a *līla* bull.
Or he may choose a fair-complexioned maiden as his wife, or he may perform the Śravaṇa vow, or he mutters [the mantra] until the end.

Then the Blessed Lord Brahmā said: "One obtains the fruit in the *Saṃhitā*. One who causes eight Brahmins to properly master it shall become wise, live for a hundred years, and acquire the Veda along with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*)."
The aged Vasu spoke of the supreme treasure to his sons:
"This is the wealth of the noble ones—namely, the sacred mantras and the vows."
"Salutations, salutations, and the mantras, and the vows—salutations, salutations!
All this is the praise of the Brahman-Pranava; in the Kaṇva recension, it concludes with 'pāraya' (lead us across)."
Thus ends the Itihāsopaniṣad.
What is given especially at the time of a Śrāddha becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors. Moving with the speed of thought, coming hither... crossing over to the further shore.
Having gone to heaven as a well-winged bird, you who [seek] the great Soma...
You are the well-winged Garuḍa; go to heaven, fly to the light!
O Tilajyotis, who art thirtyfold, fall as rain from the sky for Vṛṣādarvi.
